narrative.text: Fig. 1, 'Product master data'. A health product, drawn as a boxed medicine package, is linked to PRODUCT MASTER DATA, shown as four categories with examples. General Information: product identifier, name, description, unit of measure. Classification: ICD, ATC, product characteristics/specifications. Pharmaceutical Information: dosage, strength, route of administration, doses per vial. Logistical Information: packaging, volumetrics, shelf life, storage temperature.

basis.saw: Fig. 2, partners and processes both feeding a central product-master-data column, flowing down to patients

narrative.text: Fig. 2, 'Importance of product master data'. Three columns. On the left, SUPPLY CHAIN PARTNERS: manufacturers, procurers, Ministry of Health / programmes, donors, shippers, regulatory authority, central/regional/district warehouses and health facilities. On the right, SUPPLY CHAIN PROCESSES: forecasting and supply planning, procurement, ordering/re-ordering, inventory management, distribution, dispensing, product recalls and finance/insurance. Arrows from both point into the central PRODUCT MASTER DATA column — general information, classification details, pharmaceutical information, logistical information and other information — which flows down through a medicine icon to Patients.

narrative.text: Fig. 3, 'Impact of inconsistent product information'. An arrow labelled PHYSICAL FLOW OF HEALTH PRODUCTS runs across five actors: manufacturers, central warehouse, health facilities, community health workers and patients. Beneath them sit the systems each stage uses — a warehouse management system, an eLMIS and paper forms — and each holds the same product under a different code (123123, A1232, P44545, AM545). Broken-chain icons join the codes, showing that the identifiers do not link up along the chain.

narrative.text: Fig. 4, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases — assessing the current state and enabling environment; establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; defining the future state; planning the enterprise architecture; determining health content requirements; M&E and fostering data use; and implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. Resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, among them the DIIG, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, TOGAF, OpenHIE and the WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture. The tile 'WHO handbook for health product catalogue (this document)' is highlighted in phase 07. It is the same chart as Fig. 6 of the WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care, re-pointed to this document.

basis.saw: Fig. 5, the SMART Guidelines five-layer diagram with localisation and an evidence feedback loop

narrative.text: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines Approach'. A research and evidence base feeds five knowledge layers and their products: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each passes through LOCALISATION into a country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures, localised requirements, localised machine-readable code and standards, localised static digital services, and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. All feed DATA, EVIDENCE, AND IMPACT, which returns to the evidence base as EVIDENCE FROM DIGITAL IMPLEMENTATIONS.

narrative.text: Fig. 6, 'Example of an Antenatal Care Business clinical workflow with highlighted' activities. The upper part is a swimlane process in a health facility, with Client and Health worker lanes. The client arrives at the facility, then goes through registration, rapid assessment and management, a danger-signs/referral decision, pregnancy confirmation, a first-contact decision and a quick check. These lead to collecting the woman's profile and history, then an ANC assessment (check symptoms and follow-up, conduct physical exam, conduct laboratory tests and imaging), then 10. Counselling, in-facility management and treatment, with subactivities 10.1 to 10.9, then a referral decision, scheduling, and self-care in the home or community until the woman returns. The lower part enlarges activities 6 to 10. Highlighted borders mark 9 (conduct laboratory tests and imaging), 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis — the activities that involve health products.

basis.saw: Fig. 7, a layered architecture with shared/data services, an interoperability layer and supply-chain information systems

narrative.text: Fig. 7, 'Digital health supply chain architecture framework'. Top row: SHARED SERVICES, whose foundational components are facility, product (highlighted) and supplier registries; DATA SERVICES, with analytics (supply chain reports, data warehouse) and traceability (track and trace, product verification); and Digital Ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). A middle INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. Bottom: HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS — forecasting and planning, order management, warehouse management, cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing — beside External systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories).

narrative.text: Fig. 8, 'Linkage across classifications, generic products and trade items'. Three columns: CLASSIFICATION (classes or groups of diseases, pathogens or drugs); PRODUCT (name/INN, strength, dosage form, route of administration); and TRADE ITEM (unique identifier such as a GTIN, brand name, manufacturer, country of origin, packaging details, volumetrics, shelf life). The example row traces Nervous system → Analgesics → Other analgesics and antipyretics → Anilides → Paracetamol to the product 'Paracetamol 500 mg tablet'. That product branches into two manufacturers' trade items, each with its own unique IDs and pack hierarchy: a case and inner pack of 100 from ABC Manufacturing (brand Ceta123), and a case, inner pack of 50 and each of 10 from XYZ Manufacturing (brand ParaXYZ). A bottom row gives each column's use: strategic (data aggregation and analysis), tactical (forecasting, procurement planning and aggregate visibility) and operational (inventory, distribution, tracking and tracing, pharmacovigilance and AEFI analysis).

basis.saw: Fig. 9, a three-class data model with attribute cardinalities and 1-to-0..* associations

narrative.text: Fig. 9, 'Relationship between generic product, trade item and regulated trade item'. Three classes are drawn as boxes listing their attributes with cardinalities. GENERIC PRODUCT has identifier 0..*, status, name (nameType, nameValue), description, classification, unitOfUse, dosageForm, strength, routeOfAdministration, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, doseQuantity, attribute (type, value[x]) and associatedProduct (product, relationship, quantity). TRADE ITEM has identifier 1..*, status, tradeItemName, description, classification, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, associatedGenericProduct (genericProduct, quantity), contains (tradeItem, quantity) and attribute. REGULATED TRADE ITEM has identifier, status, jurisdiction, authorisationHolder, validityPeriod, authorisedTradeItem, attribute and associatedProduct. The associations read: one generic product to zero or more trade items, and one trade item to zero or more regulated trade items.

narrative.text: Fig. 13, 'Transitional approach to adopting globally unique trade item numbers'. A national product code record — NPC01101001, Lamivudine 50 mg tablet, dosage form TA, route oral — branches into two tables of trade items mapped to it. The first holds GS1 GTINs (for example 58904093825793) for manufacturer MFR001 from IN, with child GTINs, child quantities of 100 and 10, 3000 eaches and a shelf life of 670. The second holds items from MFR002 from KE that have no GTIN yet and are identified only by country trade item identifiers (P006008, P006009), with child quantities of 120 and 30, 7200 eaches and a shelf life of 1095. So a national code can carry GTIN-identified and not-yet-GTIN-identified items side by side during the transition.

narrative.text: Fig. 14, 'Illustration of how countries can leverage WHO hosted PCMT'. Inside a panel labelled PRODUCT CATALOGUE MANAGEMENT TOOL, a GLOBAL CATALOGUE (global identifier, unit of use, pharmaceutical information such as dosage form, route of administration and strength, trade item information, and manufacturer, country of origin and shelf life) feeds COUNTRY CATALOGUE A and COUNTRY CATALOGUE B, each adding country identifiers and country-specific information such as registration numbers. The arrows are annotated 'Country catalogues to derive common product information from the global catalog'. Country A Users and Country B Users each work in their own catalogue, and the whole sits on WHO INFRASTRUCTURE.

narrative.text: Fig. 15, 'Illustration of how countries can share data with the WHO hosted PCMT'. It extends Fig. 14. As there, the global catalogue feeds country catalogues A and B inside the PRODUCT CATALOGUE MANAGEMENT TOOL on WHO infrastructure, used by Country A and Country B users. In addition, each country catalogue returns 'Product master data' to the global catalogue, and OTHER COUNTRIES contribute PRODUCT MASTER DATA into it from above, so the global catalogue is fed by the countries as well as feeding them.
